label: J-Holomorphic Curves: The Central Tool
notes: This opening lecture covers printed pages 1 through 16 of McDuff and Salamon. We motivate why a single local differential equation, the nonlinear Cauchy-Riemann equation, became the organizing tool of modern symplectic topology after Gromov introduced pseudoholomorphic curves in 1985.

label: Symplectic Manifolds and the Question
notes: A symplectic manifold carries a closed nondegenerate two-form supplying signed area. The chapter question is sharp: how does a local Cauchy-Riemann type equation become a global symplectic invariant. Everything in the course is an answer pieced together from compactness, transversality, and counting machinery built later.

label: Almost Complex Structures and Taming
notes: An almost complex structure squares to minus the identity, turning each tangent space into a complex vector space. Taming demands omega of v and Jv stay positive, aligning the two structures so complex lines carry genuine positive symplectic area. This pointwise positivity underpins every later energy estimate.

label: The Nonlinear Cauchy-Riemann Equation
notes: A J-holomorphic curve is a map u from a Riemann surface into an almost complex manifold whose differential commutes with the two complex structures. The equation du composed with j equals J composed with du is the nonlinear Cauchy-Riemann equation, generalizing classical holomorphic maps to curved nonintegrable targets.

label: Gromov 1985 and Nonsqueezing
notes: Gromov introduced pseudoholomorphic curves in 1985 and immediately proved nonsqueezing: a symplectic embedding of a ball of radius r into a cylinder forces the cylinder radius to be at least r. A holomorphic disc through any point produces the area bound, turning soft topology rigid.

label: Moduli Spaces of Curves
notes: Fixing a homology class and marked points, the solutions of the Cauchy-Riemann equation form a moduli space. Studying symplectic manifolds means studying these spaces. Their geometry, not any single curve, encodes the invariants, so we must control their dimension, smoothness, and limiting behavior carefully.

label: Transversality: Regularity
notes: Transversality asks that the linearized Cauchy-Riemann operator be surjective, making the moduli space a smooth manifold of the Fredholm index dimension. For generic almost complex structures regularity holds for simple curves, so the predicted dimension is real and the count well defined rather than illusory.

label: Compactness: Controlling Limits
notes: Compactness controls how sequences of curves degenerate. Bounded energy forces convergence up to bubbling, where energy concentrates and spheres pinch off. Gromov compactness replaces missing limits by stable maps, so the moduli space has a closed, countable boundary structure suitable for intersection theory.

label: Evaluation Maps and Pseudocycles
notes: Evaluation at marked points sends a curve to its image points, turning the moduli space into a geometric cycle in the target. Because of the controlled boundary, this evaluation defines a pseudocycle that can be intersected with constraints, the bridge from analysis to enumerative geometry.

label: Gromov-Witten Invariants
notes: Gromov-Witten invariants are intersection numbers of the evaluation pseudocycle against chosen constraints once the dimension budget cancels to zero. They are deformation invariant and satisfy splitting axioms, making them robust symplectic invariants rather than artifacts of a chosen almost complex structure or metric.

label: The Strategy in One Diagram
notes: The strategy is a pipeline: the local equation defines curves, transversality gives smooth moduli, compactness gives boundaries, evaluation gives cycles, intersection gives invariants, and invariants prove theorems. Each arrow is a later chapter; the introduction is the route map connecting analysis to topology.

label: Previews and Course Map
notes: These invariants seed deeper theories: quantum cohomology deforms the cup product using genus zero counts, while Floer homology applies the same curve counting to Hamiltonian systems and Lagrangian intersections. Nonsqueezing, symplectic four-manifolds, and vortex equations follow as applications across the remaining chapters.
